justification: Contribution is a finite calculus for when step-level evaluator authorization fails to compose (EPK, gluing defects), a conceptual/formal framing the abstract says is explicitly not benchmark-validated.
Nexus's headline mechanism is an adaptive selector that picks Direct, ReAct or Plan-and-Execute per task, and it is assessed on 500 real enterprise tasks with production-deployment lessons.
Both systems contribute a decomposition of the task into editable subgoals or phases that fixes the next step, tested in a lab within-subjects study (n=18) rather than in deployed practice.
CARA is a family of automated metrics that audit reasoning alignment in debate and name the 'consistency illusion' failure mode; evidence is lab runs on MedQA-USMLE and MedThink-Bench.
The contribution is the modular arrangement of interpretation, synthesis, validation and correction agents itself; the abstract argues for the pipeline and reports no measured study.
XPS 2's mechanism is a symbolic controller that must verify every LLM hypothesis before it can influence a decision; the paper outlines the architecture and demonstrates it on fault diagnosis only.
The claim concerns the arrangement of role-differentiated agents in shared context and prescribes injecting an isolated external agent; it is argued as a governance requirement with no study.

The paper's stated distinguishing element is an integrated monitor combining internal reasoning with execution results to detect abnormal behaviour; evaluated on task scenarios in a lab workflow environment.
A heuristic synthesis arguing that coordination topology determines failure geometry across agent networks; it offers a structural reading and a falsification path, not its own evidence.

TUMIX's claim is the composition of the agent ensemble - which tool-use strategies and how many agents, auto-optimized - and it is validated on reasoning benchmarks against test-time-scaling baselines.

SI-Agent's loop rewrites the system instruction itself from reward-agent feedback across cycles, an outer self-improvement loop; evidence is lab experiments on performance, readability and efficiency versus baselines.
The mechanism is refining the prompt from the output-versus-target error until criteria are met, framed via controllers; the paper supplies a mathematical foundation and no evaluation.
Agent-R constructs self-critique training data from its own MCTS trajectories and iteratively retrains the agent to reflect; validated in three interactive environments in the lab.
Retroformer learns a retrospective model by policy gradient that rewrites the agent's prompt from environment rewards across episodes; results are lab task suites against non-gradient baselines.
MOSAIC structures inference as plan, check, then act-or-refuse with refusal as a first-class gate on tool actions; evaluated zero-shot on out-of-distribution safety benchmarks, not in deployment.
The contribution is reward design that suppresses excessive tool calls (72% fewer) to cut latency while keeping the trajectory shape; evidence is lab experiments across reasoning and QA domains.
IterInject's novelty is the refinement step: a diagnoser's structured outcome labels drive an optimizer that rewrites payloads over history; measured on AgentDojo and InjectAgent in the lab.

The study tests whether iterating on experimental feedback actually improves the agent's next hypotheses, with a permuted-feedback control over 800 replications - a lab audit of the revise-on-feedback step.
The artefact is a 180-task ABAP benchmark used to measure several LLMs, including how well compiler feedback drives iterations; all runs are lab benchmarking of existing models.
ToolBench-X is an instrument: executable tasks with five injected hazard types and recovery paths for measuring agent loops, evaluated on existing agents in the lab.
MINT is a benchmark and harness for measuring multi-turn tool use and language feedback across 20 LLMs, an instrument rather than a loop mechanism, run entirely in the lab.
DGM is an outer loop in which the agent rewrites its own code and archives variants across generations; the claim is validated by SWE-bench and Polyglot scores against non-self-improving baselines.
MARS's distinguishing mechanism is memory optimization with an Ebbinghaus forgetting curve for long-span information; the abstract asserts improvement without reporting any study.
CER's mechanism is a dynamic buffer that accumulates and retrieves distilled past experience into the context window, training-free; validated on WebArena and VisualWebArena in the lab.
ERL stores reflection-derived heuristics and retrieves the relevant ones into context, with ablations crediting selective retrieval; evidence is Gaia2 benchmark runs against a ReAct baseline.
